description: Basic algebraic language for unital commutative rings and fields, including ideals, maximal ideals, residue fields, fraction fields, characteristic, and prime fields.

Standard structure theory for Z, Q, finite fields, and polynomial rings over finite fields: fundamental theorem of arithmetic, unique factorization of rationals, existence of finite fields F_q, irreducible-polynomial quotients F_q[t]/(f), and the basic comparison between number fields and global function fields.
Classical real and local-field background: the usual absolute value on Q inherited from R, completions with respect to absolute values, and the existence of the p-adic fields Q_p.
Characteristic-p and finite-field identities used without proof, especially n^p = n in F_p and x^q = x in a finite field of cardinality q.
The p-adic absolute value is a well-defined absolute value on Q, which requires the standard valuation arithmetic v_p(xy) = v_p(x) + v_p(y) and v_p(x + y) >= min(v_p(x), v_p(y)).

Ostrowski's theorem classifying the nontrivial absolute values on Q up to equivalence; the text explicitly defers the proof to Problem Set 1 and cites Chapter 1 of reference [3] for much of the section.
The product formula on Q depends on unique prime factorization and the fact that only finitely many places p <= infinity contribute nontrivially to the product for a fixed x in Q^times.

Standard commutative-algebra background on integral domains and their fraction fields, ideals and principal ideals, units, maximal and prime ideals, local rings and residue fields, localization, principal ideal domains, unique factorization domains, and the basic vocabulary of noetherian, regular, one-dimensional, and integrally closed rings.

Basic valuation-theory facts used without proof: a valuation v on a field yields a nonarchimedean absolute value via c^v, every discrete subgroup of R is infinite cyclic and can be rescaled to Z, valuation rings are local with unit group {x : v(x) = 0}, and in a DVR every nonzero ideal is a power of the maximal ideal generated by any uniformizer.
Classical arithmetic example of a DVR obtained by localizing Z at a prime ideal: the local ring Z_(p), its maximal ideal (p), and the identification of the residue field Z_(p)/p Z_(p) with F_p.
Formal Laurent-series and power-series background: the fields k((t)), rings k[[t]], the t-adic order of vanishing, and Laurent-series expansions of rational functions around a point alpha.

The classification theorem that the usual properties listed in the text are equivalent characterizations of discrete valuation rings; the proof is explicitly deferred to references [1, §23] and [2, §9].

Standard algebra used in the proof that sums and products of integral elements remain integral: existence of an algebraic closure of the fraction field, factorization of monic polynomials there, and the fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials expressing coefficients of \prod_{i,j}(z-(alpha_i+beta_j)) and \prod_{i,j}(z-alpha_i beta_j) as polynomials in the coefficients of the original monic polynomials.
